expectations.evidence: outputs/council-prompts.md exists (67,305 bytes, 793 lines). Contains exactly 3 deliberator prompts: Pragmatist (line 113 'You are the **Pragmatist**...'), Stress Tester (line 259), Falsifier (line 405). Independent grep confirms exactly 3 occurrences each of '**Your value function:**', '## Your lens', '## Research directives', '## Problem', and '## Context' -- one full set per role, none missing or duplicated. Header table (line 7: '**Tier** | Moderate') and Gate 2 (line 35: 'Gate 2 -- tier (Moderate, as requested)') both state Moderate tier, and the per-agent research budget stated in all 3 prompts (line 201/347/493: '~20,000 tokens for this round') matches SKILL.md's own Moderate-tier table value ('Tool budget/agent: ~20k'). Directly diffed the value function / lens / research-directives text against references/roles/pragmatist.md, stress-tester.md, and falsifier.md -- byte-identical in all 3 cases, confirming the prompts are genuinely populated from the real role library, not paraphrased or fabricated.

Independent grep for the exact token list `\[(GOAL|CONTEXT|ROLE_NAME|VALUE_FUNCTION|ROLE_LENS|RESEARCH_DIRECTIVES|TOKEN_BUDGET|MODE|LEAD_NAME)\]` against the output file returns zero matches. A broader scan for any bracketed ALL-CAPS token `\[[A-Z_]{3,}\]` also returns zero matches. facts.json independently confirms `"placeholders_left": []`. Note: the file does contain bracketed notes like '[LEAD: paste the "Recommended approach" ... sections of the Proposal Document, verbatim.]' (line 656) and '[LEAD: paste the same Codebase-facts block ...]' (line 660) inside the pre-mortem prompt -- these are not unfilled generation-time template tokens (none matches the forbidden list), they are intentional runtime-fill markers for content that cannot exist until after the human has actually run the council, structurally identical to the intentional '___' blanks in the Codebase-facts block (items 1-11).

claims.claim: Total package length is approximately 10,200-10,500 words (~67KB, 793 lines)
claims.evidence: facts.json reports 10,220 words; independent `wc -w` on the output file reports 10,485 words (minor tokenizer-methodology difference, not a discrepancy of substance); `wc -c` confirms 67,305 bytes.

usability_note: Total package size: ~10,200-10,500 words (~67KB, 793 lines) -- confirmed via facts.json and independent wc -w/-c. A human could realistically paste this into Claude.ai as designed: the document is not meant to be pasted whole, it decomposes into 5 clearly fenced, individually copy-pasteable blocks (3 deliberator prompts + Red-Team prompt + optional Lead-assistant prompt), each ranging roughly 600-2,500 words -- well within a single Claude.ai message. Fences use 4-backtick delimiters for every 'paste into its own chat' block versus plain 3-backtick delimiters for illustrative-only templates (Round 1 Digest format, Proposal Document format), which is a correct and deliberate defensive-markdown choice. The large total word count is driven almost entirely by necessary duplication -- each deliberator prompt independently repeats the full Problem, Context, Codebase-facts block, and tooling/budget/citation boilerplate, because each will run in an isolated Claude.ai chat with no shared memory -- not by padding. The package is honest about its own overhead: it budgets '30-60 minutes' of human prep time and '2-3 hours end-to-end' up front (Section 0), and instructs the lead to fill the Codebase-facts block once and paste it into all three chats. Net assessment: usable as designed, with the caveat that a human must correctly propagate the same Codebase-facts answers into 3 separate chats and keep them in sync if corrected at Checkpoint 1 -- a manual-sync risk the package acknowledges but cannot eliminate given the human-orchestrated, no-shared-state design mode.

suggestions.assertion: Chosen roles include at least one pair listed as 'natural tension' in roles-index.md
suggestions.reason: The bar is low: a 3-role council satisfies this with exactly one tension pair while a third role sits in tension with neither, seated without any justification, and would still pass. This run happens to go further -- it explicitly justifies Falsifier's seat despite Falsifier not being roles-index.md-listed as in tension with Pragmatist or Stress Tester -- but the assertion doesn't require that reasoning. Consider strengthening to: 'every seated role is either in a listed tension pair with another seat, or its inclusion is explicitly justified in the composition rationale.'

No assertion checks that the Problem/Goal and Context sections faithfully carry the user's actual constraints (10-week deadline, 6-person team, ~40 tenant-scoped SQLAlchemy models, the senior engineer's stated RLS preference, the two tradeoffs verbatim). A run that produced 3 well-formed but genericized deliberator prompts -- e.g. dropping the deadline, or omitting the organizational fact about the senior engineer -- would pass all 6 existing expectations unchanged. I manually verified this run's Problem/Context sections do carry every constraint faithfully (cross-checked against the Step 1 task text), but no assertion covers this and it is exactly the kind of silent content-fidelity failure a weaker run could produce undetected.

No assertion checks that the per-agent token budget populated in the prompts is numerically consistent with the stated tier's own definition (SKILL.md: Moderate = ~20k/agent). This run gets it exactly right (verified independently against SKILL.md's tier table), but expectation 1's '(Moderate tier)' parenthetical only checks that the tier label is present somewhere in the file, not that the budget number the prompts actually instruct deliberators to use matches that tier. A run that labeled itself Moderate while quietly populating a Complex-tier budget (~35k) would still pass as written.

eval_feedback.overall: All 6 expectations passed on genuine, independently-verified evidence, not surface-level compliance -- I diffed the exported value functions/lenses/research-directives byte-for-byte against the source role files, cross-checked the token-budget and total-cost figures against SKILL.md's own tier and modifier tables, and grepped the raw transcript for Agent/subagent_type tool calls myself rather than trusting facts.json's or the transcript's self-report. This is a well-executed run: the design-mode adaptation (translating SendMessage/subagent/teammate mechanics into human-copy-paste instructions) is coherent and internally consistent, the Round 2 anti-sycophancy examples are custom-written per role rather than boilerplate, and the executor was transparent about a tier-boundary judgment call rather than inflating justification. The main gap in the expectations as written: none of them checks semantic fidelity of the Problem/Context to the user's actual stated constraints, and none checks numeric consistency between the declared tier and the budget/cost figures the package derives from it -- both happened to hold up perfectly here under manual inspection, but a run that got either wrong would still pass all 6 assertions.
